newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian companies prepare for arrival of euro.
newsitem.headline: Belgian companies prepare for arrival of euro.

text.p: Belgian companies are preparing to change their statutes to permit them to express their capital in the European single currency even though it is not due to be launched for two years.
Banque Bruxelles Lambert is believed to be the first company planning to modify its articles in this way.
At an extraordinary general meeting on April 30 shareholders will be asked to clear the way for the capital of the bank to be stated in euros from the moment the currency "enters into circulation."
The same wording has been followed by Belgian property company Bernheim-Comofi, which is proposing a similar change to shareholders on May 12.

A BBL spokeswoman said the bank was carrying out the change now, rather than waiting until next year after European Union leaders pick the countries taking part in economic and monetary union (EMU), because it had to be voted on at an extraordinary general meeting (EGM).
"We don't know now if we will have an EGM next year," she said.
Bernheim-Comofi company lawyer Louis de Halleux noted, however, the companies were still taking a risk by moving in a legal grey area.

"We are still waiting for official guidance on the matter so we are doing it in the hope it will suffice and cover forthcoming legislation," de Halleux told Reuters. "Perhaps it won't do, but we can't do better for the moment."

He noted companies moving now would have to change their capital in line with the conversion rates agreed by the EU in 1998. EU officials have already said conversion rates will be six digits long, but have not clearly addressed the issue of rounding.
"We could end up with a very bizarre number for our capital unless there is some form of rounding," de Halleux said.
The BBL spokeswoman said no decision had yet been taken on rounding, but that it was not a major issue.

Both Bernheim-Comofi and BBL said they took the expression "enters into force" to mean January 1, 1999, from when the euro is due to be used in the capital markets and not January 1, 2002, when it is due to replace notes and coins in circulation.
Both companies had been advised on the wording of their statutes by Belgian notary Gilberte Raucq, they said.

In a notice published by Belgium's Accounting Standards Commission in February, Belgian companies have already been given the green light to draw up their statutory accounts -- the ones used for national tax purposes -- in euros from January 1, 1999.
"We were the first organisation at a European level to give a formal opinion on the euro," Accounting Standards Commission expert Laurence Pinte told Reuters.

She said the group was now preparing to publish a second notice coverying consolidated accounts. This would open the way for companies releasing 1998 results in early 1999 to express them in euros, she said.
"We are, however, waiting for the EU to take a formal position on a number of issues before publishing it," she said.
